newsitem.title: USA: Duke sees any Q4 impact minimal from nukes.
newsitem.headline: Duke sees any Q4 impact minimal from nukes.

text.p: A Duke Power Co spokesman said Thursday any impact to fourth-quarter earnings as a result of downed utility stations would be minimal.

Duke was forced to start shutting down its McGuire nuclear power units 1 and 2 after one of the facility's four battery banks failed to meet performance criteria during a recent test. They were expected to be down for at least three weeks.
Also, the company's Oconee nuclear facility remained closed after a steam pipe rupture in September that scalded some employees. The three units were due to reopen by January.
"If there is an impact, it will be small," said Duke Power spokesman Randy Wheeless told Reuters. "I can't put a dollar figure or a cents-per-share on that."

The McGuire units are based in Cornelius, N.C. and have a combined generation capacity of 2,258 megawatts (MW), while the power units at Oconee in Seneca, S.C. produce a combined 2,538 MW of electricity.

"A lot depends on how much power and what kind of prices we have to buy in the short term. We're lucky in the sense that this is a relatively mild time of year, so our need isn't as great as if this were the middle of summer," Wheeless said.
Duke Power, based here, operates in central and western North Carolina as well as upstate South Carolina, where the weather has been uncharacteristically warm the past weeks.
"But we don't know today what the weather looks like for the next few weeks," Wheeless said.
Janney Montgomery Scott analyst David Schanzer said there was plenty of power available for sale to Duke.
"There's a plethora of replacement power so the prices are pretty reasonable," Schanzer said.
Peak non-firm power was talked at $25 to $26 per MW hour, unchanged from Wednesday's discussion in the cash market.
Duke said it did not anticipate problems meeting electricity demand from its customers because it was running fossil-fuel units full out.
It said it had a replacement battery bank on order for the McGuire units. The batteries provide backup power to the McGuire facility's safety and control systems.
Nuclear generation, though only one-third of Duke's overall generation capacity, typically accounts for about two-thirds of the power it puts on the grid.
The McGuire and Oconee units together represent about 26 percent of Duke's overall 18,500 MW of generation capacity.
Duke reported third-quarter results last week of $1.25 per share, down $0.08 from the $1.33 earned in the same quarter a year ago.
The decrease, in part, resulted from lower electricity sales and planned start-up costs associated with its investment in personal communications services.
